column2: Yes, when required. All ships arriving at organized quarantine stations (including those at Halifax and Saint John) when coming from countries not regarded as coastwise under the Canadian quarantine regulations are inspected every six months for evidence of rat infestation. If such vessels are infested with rats they are ordered fumigated.
Fumigations at Saint John, New Brunswick, and Halifax, Nova Scotia, are carried

column1: out by the staff of the quarantine service of this department.

column2: No insecticides are used but the fumigating gas used to kill rats has the effect of killing insects as well as mammals. The only gas suitable for fumigation purposes cannot be obtained locally.
Yes, two vessels, one of which was fumigated twice.
This work was performed by the quarantine service of this department without charge, except a total of $50 for staff working overtime during the fiscal year 1951-52.

Drew (Leader of ihe Opposition):,Leader of the Official Opposition,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,REFERENCE TO AMENDMENT OF CIVIL SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT,,Mr. Speaker, I Should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister, based upon the announcement he made a few days ago about the remaining legislation. I do so, because of certain comments that have been made with regard to amendment of the Civil Service Superannuation Act which was announced in the speech from the throne. If it is the intention of the government not to proceed with that act, and that is indicated by the omission from the reference, it would seem that there should be some explanation not only for the members of the house but
[Mr. Poullot.j
also for the civil servants who have been counting on some action with regard to this measure since the speech from the throne was read.

,Progressive Conservative,,George Alexander Drew,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=ab0b620e-8a27-4620-8601-ad7c8704c5ce&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693363,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.18.1.3,1952-06-11,4147128e-2ec6-4295-95ae-389b95cc3ca4,ca.m.9666,Hon. Douglas Abboil (Minisier of Finance):,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE,REFERENCE TO AMENDMENT OF CIVIL SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACT,,Perhaps I might answer that question, Mr. Speaker. For some time the officers of my department, the civil service commission and others have been engaged in a general revision of the superannuation act. It was not contemplated that there would be, if I may so refer to it, a major change in policy so far as the scale of superannuation is concerned, but it is a comprehensive revision of the act. Unfortunately it has not been possible to complete that job. As the house knows, there is an unofficial advisory committee. It was desired to obtain the views of that committee, and they have been consulted. Unfortunately it would not be possible to bring in the bill within the next three or four weeks. Under those circumstances it was felt that it would perhaps have to stand.

,Liberal,,Douglas Charles Abbott,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=4147128e-2ec6-4295-95ae-389b95cc3ca4&Language=E&Section=ALL

1693368,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.19.1.1.2,1952-06-11,62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443,ca.m.5390,Mr. Clarence Gillis (Cape Breton South):,,POTATOES,REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT,IMPORTATION OF U.S. POTATOES,Mr. Speaker, if I may be permitted to do so, I should like to direct a question to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Agriculture. Has the parliamentary assistant's attention been drawn to a press release in this morning's Globe and Mail stating ""federal order dashes the hope of cheaper spuds""? If so, can the parliamentary assistant inform the house whether the federal Department of Agriculture has issued an order restricting the importation of United States potatoes, thereby aggravating the already short supply in this country?

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Clarence Gillis,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=62287d4a-32a2-4734-a1b3-18cce52da443&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693369,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.19.1.1.3,1952-06-11,df7811f7-f9f8-4cec-b8b9-8f0cf68df631,ca.m.1778,Mr. Robert McCubbin (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture):,Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Agriculture,POTATOES,REFERENCE TO PRESS REPORT,IMPORTATION OF U.S. POTATOES,Mr. Speaker, in answer to the hon. member for Cape Breton South, may I say that I have seen the article in the Toronto Globe and Mail to which he refers. The story is this. Under the fruit and vegetable act, United States grade A potatoes are allowed to come into Canada duty free except for a six weeks' period; but owing to the shortage of potatoes in Canada about the middle of April those restrictions were relaxed a little bit and some grade B potatoes were allowed to come in with the grade A potatoes.
That has been changed as of tomorrow, when they go back under the fruit and vegetable act under which we just allow grade A potatoes to come in. But certainly

no restriction is placed upon potatoes coming into Canada from the United States. I can assure the hon. member that during these last few weeks potatoes have been coming into Canada from the United States at the rate of 100 cars per week. I can go further than that and say I feel that after the next few weeks potato prices will become lower.

,Liberal,,Robert McCubbin,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=df7811f7-f9f8-4cec-b8b9-8f0cf68df631&Language=E&Section=ALL

Diefenbaker (Lake Centre):,,NATIONAL DEFENCE,"CONSTRUCTION OF ROAD THROUGH SASKATOON, EDMONTON AND YELLOWHEAD",,"Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence in connection with certain representations made by the highway system association of Edmonton and also the cities of Saskatoon, North Battleford and the like. Has consideration been given to any request on the part of this association that the Department of National Defence, without in any way interfering with the trans-Canada highway location as at present decided upon, should do something to assure a defence road through Saskatoon and Edmonton and thence through Yellowhead, with a view to assuring transportation for oil and mineral development in the north?

1693379,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.21.1.3,1952-06-11,647c88fa-1673-4147-88b3-b42105bc54e3,ca.m.2918,Hon. Brooke Claxion (Minister of National Defence):,Minister of National Defence,NATIONAL DEFENCE,CONSTRUCTION OF ROAD THROUGH SASKATOON, EDMONTON AND YELLOWHEAD",,"Mr. Speaker, the hon. member was good enough to give me notice of this question, but I received it only a few minutes before three o'clock. In the time available since then I have found a reference to only one such representation. That was made by the board of trade of the city of North Battleford. They referred to a resolution of the city council and board of trade of Yellowhead and so far I have not found any record of securing such resolution.

A few days ago my colleague the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) reported to me that he had seen the executive of the Yellowhead road association and that they had made and would make representations along those lines. Of course any such representations would receive most careful consideration. I can say this, however. We have had a large number of representations from every part of Canada that we should give assistance to the construction of highways on the score that they might be useful for defence purposes. The general answer is that any increase in transportation or communication facilities would, of course, increase our capacity for defence but that unless the circumstances are extremely unusual, we have so many more projects having a greater priority and which cannot be tackled at the present time, that assistance to a highway of this character would be extremely unlikely.

Has the government been made aware of dissatisfaction on the part of a large section of ICAO with reference to the rent charged for office space in Canada, and certain other conditions? Is the government attempting to meet these objections and keep ICAO in Canada?

1693384,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.22.1.3,1952-06-11,51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f,ca.m.6889,Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):,Secretary of State for External Affairs,CIVIL AVIATION ORGANIZATION,REPORTED DISSATISFACTION OVER RENT FOR OFFICE SPACE, ETC.",,"The hon. member was good enough, as he has indicated, to give notice of this question yesterday. I have been looking into the matter, which is one of some importance because it affects the possibility of this United Nations specialized agency remaining in Montreal.
The government is aware of the fact that for some time now certain members of the

Inquiries of the Ministry International Civil Aviation Organization have felt that the rent paid by the organization for its offices in Montreal is high, not in comparison with commercial rentals in Montreal or possibly elsewhere, but in comparison with the rents paid by other specialized agencies of the United Nations, especially in countries where substantial concessions are often given to such organizations by governments in order to retain the headquarters of those organizations in their countries. The government has therefore been considering the problem, and has decided that there should be an increase in the assistance we have previously given to ICAO by way of subsidy on its rent. We proposed to ICAO on May 28 last that, subject to the approval of parliament, the rent should be reduced by the amount of $130,530 per annum. An amount to cover this will be placed in the supplementary estimates. This reduction would cut the rental rate per square foot from the present figure of $2.50 to $1, and would make it reasonably comparable with rates of rent paid by United Nations specialized agencies elsewhere.

The government is very glad to have ICAO in Montreal, and would like to see it remain there. We will be happy to consider favourably any reasonable assistance we can give to the organization for that purpose. However, some of the organization's requests do not fall within federal jurisdiction. For instance, ICAO now has requests before the government of the province of Quebec and the council of the city of Montreal for remission of certain provincial and municipal taxes. We hope that mutually satisfactory arrangements about these matters can be reached by ICAO with the authorities concerned.

,Liberal,,Lester Bowles Pearson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Progressive Conservative,,Gordon Graydon,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=795045ac-0a2d-489d-aac6-1477f9c815d1&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693386,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.22.1.5,1952-06-11,51c861ef-0f17-4a79-8d9b-0854fb3ef33f,ca.m.6889,Mr. Pearson:,Secretary of State for External Affairs,CIVIL AVIATION ORGANIZATION,REPORTED DISSATISFACTION OVER RENT FOR OFFICE SPACE, ETC.",,"I have not the exact figure, but a very considerable number, both as members of the permanent staff of ICAO who make their residence in Montreal, and as delegates from the member countries to the various meetings of ICAO.

Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) moved,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,WAR RISKS INSURANCE,ESTABLISHMENT OF MARINE AND AVIATION ACCOUNT,,that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:

1693420,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.26.1.4,1952-06-11,4147128e-2ec6-4295-95ae-389b95cc3ca4,ca.m.9666,Mr. Abbott:,Minister of Finance and Receiver General,WAR RISKS INSURANCE,ESTABLISHMENT OF MARINE AND AVIATION ACCOUNT,,Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the proposed measure to be founded upon the resolution is to authorize the Minister of Finance to enter into agreements, subject of course to approval in detail by the governor in council, for insurance and reinsurance against certain risks of loss or damage in connection with ships, aircraft and cargo, arising out of war risks.

As the committee is probably aware, insurance companies have never considered that they could underwrite war risks. They have held the view that such risks were not susceptible to actuarial calculation; and consequently those risks are always reinsured with government.

During the last war in the United Kingdom they formed what was colloquially known as the insurance association, or clubs. These clubs wrote the insurance, and it was reinsured with the United Kingdom government. Canadian shipping at that time was insured with these clubs.

Now the Canadian merchant marine has reached the point where it would be quite feasible to form an association of ship owners-which I shall refer to as a club- provided facilities are available for reinsurance with the Canadian government, as was the case with the United Kingdom government during the last war.

Obviously there are some advantages in having our own reinsurance, because the insurance proceeds would need to be paid in Canadian dollars. Ship owners would find it easier to deal with insurers who were
War Risks Insurance

available here in Canada rather than abroad, so far as the adjustment of claims and that sort of thing is concerned. This matter was discussed with the British association, which was good enough to send someone out here to go into the technical details with our own insurers.

The matter was discussed with Canadian ship owners, who have decided to form one of these associations. I understand the bill to incorporate this voluntary association is now before the other place. The matter was also examined by the maritime commission, and the enabling bill which will be based upon this resolution is to implement that decision.

The pattern will be substantially the same as was followed in the United Kingdom during the last war, except that the club-that is, the voluntary insurance association-will be formed here in Canada and the reinsurer will be the Canadian government. I am informed similar arrangements are either in force in the United Kingdom and in the United States or are in process of being formed.

The provision is a stand-by provision. It would not be availed of, except under conditions of emergency. But, as the committee will appreciate, once war breaks out or is apprehended ship owners will not allow their ships to sail. Those ships stay in port. So it is therefore essential that machinery be available for the prompt writing of war risks in the event of an emergency.

There is of course the question of the establishment of reinsurance rates. I am informed that during the last war the practice was that the rates would be fixed for three months. Policies would be issued for a three-months period; and if it was decided that the rate bad to be increased the new rates would be enforced for a further period of three months.

Fleming (Eglinlon):,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,"ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"Mr. Speaker, there are some bills which come before the house Where the principle admits of very little difference of Opinion and where the house may be expected to be in a position to confine its discussion on second reading to a short space of time and devote its major effort to a review of the clauses of the bill in committee of the whole. Such, it seemed to some of us, was the nature of the present bill; but the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) apparently thought otherwise for last night in moving second reading of the bill he read a statement for fifty minutes and conducted what I heard one member of the house call ""a one-man filibuster against his own bill"". The minister seems determined to force a debate on second reading of this measure.

I wish to say very definitely that the principle of the Combines Investigation Act is not in dispute, and I do not think it has been at any time. The principle of the legislation is well recognized and generally supported, and it does not take a long philosophical treatise, such as that to which we listened during the first half of the minister's remarks last night, to add anything to the defence of a principle which does not need any defence in this house. I think what we are looking for in the house with respect to a measure like the present bill to amend the act is means for making the legislation more effective to serve the end of maintaining competition. That is the principle of the act, and I understand that is the principle of the present bill to amend the act. If that is so, the principle does not require any extended defence in this house.

The minister has properly said that free enterprise does require the maintenance of conditions of competition. I do not think anyone quarrels with that. Certainly wherever combines exist to the public detriment then certainly there must be legislation of this kind, and there must be effective enforcement of legislation of this kind. The act very properly directs its aim at mergers, trusts and monopolies which operate or are likely to operate to the detriment or against the interests of the public, whether consumers, producers or others. In that very broad definition I think we have a picture of the purpose of this legislation, and so far as I know no one takes issue with that purpose.

The relationship of monopoly to this subject has been dealt with by the MacQuarrie committee, particularly at pages 22 to 24 of its report. I do not think any useful purpose can be served today by an extended review of what the committee had to say on that subject. Competition is of the essence of the system of free responsible enterprise

Combines Investigation Act which the overwhelming majority of the members of the house, and I am sure the overwhelming majority of Canadians, support. They want to see that system maintained and they want to see it strengthened.

Economic freedom within that kind of system has a very direct bearing upon political freedom. You cannot dissociate the two. In that respect I think the minister was on very sound ground last night. We endanger and jeopardize the political freedom that we associate with democracy wherever there is a tampering with or trespassing upon the freedom in economic affairs which we associate with conditions of competition.

Where a government intervenes in the interests of preserving conditions of competition, Mr. Speaker, it must be on the basis of fairness; and when the government embarks upon proposals for extensive changes in legislation in this field it therefore ought to be very sure that it is proceeding fairly. That is the reason why, when the amendments proposed to this act last fall were before the house and the committee, we of the official opposition urged most strenuously that we should be very sure we had before us all the available evidence. That is why we took strenuous objection to the procedure then followed, which had the effect of stopping many people and organizations who had representations to make to the committee on that subject and denying them the opportunity of being heard.

I intend that the comments I make on the bill shall be brief. The principal change in the present act proposed by the bill is aimed to bring about a separation of the functions which are now entrusted to the commissioner under the Combines Investigation Act. When the resolution preceding the bill was before the house there was a discussion about the contradiction in his functions at the present time. He is both policeman and to some extent judge as well, certainly judge in the sense of giving a preliminary decision. That contradiction in functions has been recognized by the MacQuarrie committee, and it seems to me that this legislation, in proposing the separation of those functions, is sound in its purpose. The director will hereafter be charged with responsibility for investigation and research whereas the commission will be charged with responsibility for review, appraisal and report.

In some respects this division of functions represents a legislative return to the situation that obtained in 1923, and the departure from that position, which resulted when the then registrar, Mr. McGregor, was made commissioner, is now being reversed. I do not think the change made in 1923 was sound;
Combines Investigation Act therefore I welcome this reversal of the legislative position, this separation of functions, which is the chief characteristic of the present bill.

The second point that I think may merit a word of observation relates to the provisions of the bill with regard to the effect of the tariff in situations where it may have the effect of assisting in the maintenance of monopolistic conditions. In his speech last night the minister gave the reasons why the government has not seen fit to propose the adoption of the recommendation of the MacQuarrie committee in this regard. At this point I am not going to make further comment on the subject, because the section will be before the committee shortly. But I do express, Mr. Speaker, a question as to why the tariff board, which is an excellent board, has not been used more widely in this respect. One would have thought that where there is a suggestion or suspicion that a tariff is contributing to the creation or maintenance of monopolistic conditions or is tending to reduce the free play of competition, the tariff board would be the proper body to which a reference would be directed. I suggest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) that the tariff board could be put to very good use in such a situation.

The third point that may justify comment is the subject of research. I thought I had indicated my views on this matter when speaking on the resolution stage on June 2. Last night the Minister of Justice invited me to make some further clarification in this regard. Let me leave no doubt as to my views on the matter. I believe the proposal to vest in the director of investigations the function of research is good. There is much to be said for carrying on research in this whole field. The nub of the matter, of course, will be the competence of the hands in which that function of research is placed. It seems to me that is the whole sum and substance of this matter.

The fourth subject worthy of comment, Mr. Speaker, relates to the proposed innovation in the act in the introduction of court orders of prohibition. Because these are to be orders obtained from a court and not orders that may be issued by a governmental official, I think we may be assured that ample judicial safeguards will be attached to the issuance of such orders. It is a very wide power, and I think for that reason all hon. members ought to be glad to see it vested in a court rather than in a government official. I must confess to feeling a little disquiet in regard to the constitutionality of this provision, in the light of what the minister had to say about it last

night. He said, as his words appear at page 3118 of Hansard, that this question of the constitutionality of this section had been considered by the law officers of his department, and that they had expressed ""strong reason for believing that the section is within federal competence.""

One can only hope that when parliament is legislating to this effect, parliament is acting within its proper sphere of legislative competence. In view of the air of doubt attached to the matter, I think the minister might well consider whether this matter should not be referred to the courts for a decision. If it is not, I presume we will be on common ground in thinking it may arrive in the highest court in this country for a decision before very long, when the jurisdiction is exercised.

There is a further aspect of this matter which is of importance for those of us who recall the experience of 1949. It has to do with the subject of publicizing reports. When this measure was at the resolution stage I drew attention to the view expressed by the MacQuarrie committee that the present provision of the act with relation to the publicizing of reports should be continued. In speaking at page 2817 of Hansard for June 2, I had this to say:

... I trust that, in keeping with the recommendations of the MacQuarrie committee, this new legislation will not subtract one whit from the requirements of the present legislation with regard to publication of reports. The minister nods-
I was commenting on the nod the minister then gave me, Mr. Speaker, assenting thereby, as I thought, to the statement I had just made.
-indicating that the legislation will not tamper with that important provision of the present legislation.

With that nodding assurance from the minister, Mr. Speaker, you will understand that it was with some measure of surprise I found when the bill was distributed that the time allowed for the publication of reports of the commission had been enlarged from 15 days to 30 days. We shall have a further opportunity of discussing that section in the committee of the whole shortly, but I shall say this now. We shall want better reasons for extending this period than those given to us for the notorious and illegal extension of the 15-day period that the government wrought in 1949, when the famous McGregor report on a combine in the milling industry was tabled. The minister made no comment on this subject in his lengthy review of the bill. I believe the house will be curious to know why, especially in view of what the minister indicated to the house on June 2,
this change is attempted in this very important provision.

The next point, sir, is that the legislation is silent as to the loss leader practice. After all that was said in this house on that subject, and in a special committee of both houses last fall, I think most of us expected to see some reference to this vicious loss leader practice, but the minister has made no reference whatever to it. I observe that the Mac-Quarrie committee dismissed the subject very briefly. There are only three paragraphs on that subject on page 46 of the committee's report, and the conclusion is summed up in the third paragraph as follows:

We, therefore, propose that the ""loss leader"" practice should be referred by the minister for thorough study by the proposed agency and board with a view to determining its prevalence and its effects and to recommending to the minister suitable amendment, if necessary, of the act.

It is quite evident, sir, that the MacQuarrie committee did not consider its task completed or discharged in that respect. They have placed that problem squarely on the doorstep of the minister, and one must therefore express some disappointment that a subject so important as this vicious loss leader practice, which has such dangers in it, should have entirely escaped the minister's attention in his long speech last night.

I have no further comment upon the features of the bill, but in approving the principle of this measure on second reading I affirm what I tried to say on previous occasions, that in seeking more effective methods of maintaining conditions of competition in Canadian business and trade there is something that is more important than mere technical improvements in legislation or technical improvements in the machinery, important as those may be. More important than these is the drive behind the enforcement of the legislation. That is what we of the official opposition are demanding. It is the drive that is going to turn the wheels of this machinery which is of first importance. We may be improving the machinery. We may be adding another wheel. We may be introducing technical improvements. But, Mr. Speaker, the factor that will continue to be of first importance will be the drive behind the machinery.

I think the view of the official opposition in this matter can be summed up in this way. We want to see the maximum effectiveness and the maximum fairness in the enforcement of this act. In that respect we remind the government that it forfeited the confidence of this house and of the country in its enforcement of this legislation by what it did or failed to do in 1949, when it not only ignored but defied the plain terms of this very act. Assurances now of intention to give

Combines Investigation Act enforcement to the terms of the amendment now before the house will have to be weighed by the house in the light of that shocking and completely unjustified defiance of a statute enacted by the parliament of Canada through the suppression for ten months of a report in the very teeth of the plain terms of this legislation. For that act of suppression the whole government shared the responsibility, and it continues to do so.

It is true that the Minister of Justice, as the minister of the crown principally charged with enforcement of this legislation, bears a heavy responsibility. But to the extent to which the whole cabinet concurred in the failure of the Minister of Justice to obey the law of this land, the whole cabinet was equally responsible for an outrageous breach of the law. We had then exposed to view, on the part of 19 members of the cabinet, a submissive yielding to the determination of one member of that cabinet that that report should not be made public. He was the same minister who said in this house a year ago, ""If we wanted to get away with it, who would stop us?"" Apparently when the question of obeying the law of this land and making public the report of Mr. McGregor on the milling combine at the beginning of 1949 came before the cabinet, that same minister took just about the same attitude, an attitude which might well have been paraphrased in these words:
column2: If I want to get away with

column1: it, who in this cabinet is going to stop me?"" At any rate nobody in the cabinet stopped him. Every member of the cabinet was a party to the suppression of a report in defiance of the law of this land.

The minister spoke last night about the rule of law. Mr. Speaker, what does the rule of law mean if it does not mean that the law of this land is binding upon every person in this land from the Prime Minister to the citizen in the humblest walk of life? On that occasion apparently the attitude of the cabinet was, ""Well, the law is good enough for the rest of the country but it is not going to be binding upon us"". Sir, that was no rule of law. That was the most outrageous and palpable and deliberate attempt at the destruction of the rule of law that has been witnessed in the lifetime of the Canadian nation.

Sir, we wish to see in the administration and enforcement of this act such effectiveness as will admit of no exceptions for cabinet ministers or others; we wish to see the kind of enforcement that will demand honour and respect for the law and will give maximum effectiveness to this enactment of parliament. We of the official opposition shall make it our business to see to it that that responsibility, not only of observing the law itself
Combines Investigation Act but of giving effective enforcement to it, is honoured by the government or that failure to do so is exposed for public condemnation.

Not only did the Minister of Justice indulge in this tirade against socialism, despite the extent to which they have had to accept the idea that there are some things the community has to do for itself through the agency of government rather than leaving it to private enterprise; he also seemed to overlook the fact that this great, strong creature known as free enterprise that is supposed to stand on its own feet and do so much for the good of the country and the people generally is forever coming to the government of which my hon. friend is a minister for assistance of one kind and another.

There are tariffs, subsidies and subventions; there are freight rate adjustments, to say nothing of what is done for private enterprise by government contracts. Let me remind the minister also of the tremendous amount of assistance that so-called free private enterprise gets out of services provided by the people through their government. I could mention, for example, the post office, the dominion bureau of statistics, the national research council, the coal board, the maritime commission, the meteorological service; I could also mention aids to navigation of various kinds, the building of the trans-Canada highway and the defence highways that were asked for today, and also this matter of war
risk insurance that was brought up today. In other words, Mr. Speaker, is it not a Action to talk about free private enterprise in the terms in which the minister indulged last evening?

I must also remind the minister, who states that free private enterprise, free competition as he describes it, is a way of achieving or providing a decent standard of living for great numbers of people, that the facts belie that assertion. He knows of the great numbers of people in this country who do not pay any income tax at all because their incomes are below the very low exemption levels set by this government. Private enterprise has failed them by the millions. He knows too how necessary it has been for his government to respond to our demands for increasing measures of social legislation such as family allowances, old age pensions, and some day we hope health insurance, although it is taking a lot longer than it should to win that measure of social reform. But why do we have to win these things? Because private enterprise does not distribute the wealth that is created under it on a fair and equitable basis to the people who work under private enterprise. Thus it becomes necessary, even with the measure of social conscience that resides in some of the members of the present government, to take steps in the name of the people to correct the abuses, to correct the things that are wrong in free private enterprise and give the people of the country a little bit of a break.

Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the speech the minister made last night, the Arst half of it at any rate-and that seemed to be the part he most enjoyed giving-was ridiculous in the extreme, and that it was made in complete disregard of the facts of the situation.

As I have already said, the very fact that the minister is bringing in this bill, the very fact that we have had combines legislation on our statute books for the past 42 years, is an admission that it is inherent in the nature of capitalism, it is inherent in the nature of free private enterprise, to go in the direction of monopolistic control. It is inherent in its very nature that you get this concentration of economic power which can be and is used to deprive the workers and the farmers of a country such as ours of their fair share of the wealth they produce.

Therefore I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if the Minister of Justice felt that on some occasion he wanted to make a speech in defence of free private enterprise he certainly chose the wrong occasion when he was introducing a bill, the very introduction of which is an admission of one of the major faults of

Combines Investigation Act so-called private enterprise. In other words the bill before us, Mr. Speaker, is nothing more nor less than the admission of an avowed private enterprise Minister of Justice that the inherent nature of private enterprise is such that it works against the interests of the people of the country, and that it has to be checked by legislation of this kind.

of the fact that at least in part it implements some of the recommendations made by the MacQuarrie committee. I have already referred to the part it does implement; and we think it is a good idea to separate the differing functions connected with the combines investigation authority.

However we feel, as indeed the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has already said, that what is really important in this effort of a capitalist government to curb these capitalist emanations is the earnestness or the enthusiasm with which they pursue the terms of the legislation. As the hon. member for Eglinton has reminded the minister, we had an example in 1949 where the earnestness of that pursuit was somewhat weak, and where the minister delayed for a number of months even the tabling of a report. That means that in giving approval to the bill, as we do, at the same time we express the hope that the minister and the government will really be vigilant in trying to check these monopolistic practices.

In that connection I would point out that the MacQuarrie report is not the first occasion upon which monopolistic practices of private enterprise have been drawn to the attention of the minister and the government. That fact has been implied in practically all the reports made to the minister and the government in recent years. But I would remind the minister in particular of Mr. McGregor's report on Canada and international cartels, which was submitted to the then minister of Justice on October 10, 1945. As the hon. member knows, this is a very interesting document, and a very damning one, too, so far as private enterprise is concerned. It goes beyond the question of local domestic monopolies and deals with the part that is played in our economy and in that of the whole world by international cartels.

Mr. McGregor points out in this report that there are a number of instances where these international cartels seemed to regard themselves as above the laws of this or any other country. He also pointed out a number of instances where the people of Canada have been denied certain products, such as longlife light bulbs, and have been denied cheaper products such as radios and the like, because of the practices of international cartels.

The report of the then commissioner is very useful, and in it he made a number of very definite recommendations. In the main those recommendations are set out in the last few pages of the report. I put a number of them on record when we were debating resale price maintenance last fall, and I shall not quote them again. But I do remind the minister that very few of the suggestions made on that occasion by Mr. McGregor have

been implemented by the government since then. Some of Mr. McGregor's comments at that time are in fact re-echoed in the MacQuarrie report. Well, when the MacQuarrie committee makes that recommendation to the government, and when the Tories support it, and when, as I am sure there is, there is support from the Social Credit party, as well as from ourselves, I do not know what the minister is waiting for, or what is holding up this Liberal government. I thought the Liberals were supposed to be low-tariff or free trade people. Here we have the MacQuarrie committee and all the opposition parties in the house, including the Tories, urging action along that line, and the minister saying, ""We do not think we can deal with it in a legislative manner.""

That simply underlines the point I made a moment ago, that if we are going to place any fetters upon the monopolistic tendencies and practices of free enterprise, it will call for more than just putting legislation on the statute books. It will call for more than just a new paper organization. It will call for real vigilance and real determination on the part of the government.

1693531,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.60,1952-06-11,c2d813a5-a966-4bb3-ae3f-2aa943b5d543,ca.m.2582,Mr. Johnston:,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"The other day we had the report which was made to the Minister of

Justice (Mr. Garson) by the committee studying combines legislation. That report contains some important recommendations. One thing the report points out is that there must be constant and careful supervision to see that private enterprise does not overstep its bounds and come to that place where it becomes detrimental to public interest. I am sorry the minister has neglected to include in his legislation one of the recommendations of this committee, which was referred to by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. On page 63 of the report reference is made to tariff, patent and other remedial action, and the following recommendations are made:

column2: That the use of the tariff and patent clauses of the act should be given special consideration in cases presented before the board.

That section 29 of the act dealing with tariff action and section 30 of the act dealing with patent action be amended in order to make the requirements of the public interest the condition justifying a recommendation and action in these respects.

column1: This was referred to not long ago by the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) in connection with automobile tires. He has pointed out on a number of occasions, and I have always supported him, that a monopoly exists in this country in the rubber industry, particularly as applied to automobile tires. He has suggested on more than one occasion that one of the most effective ways of dealing with this problem would be through the tariff. The minister made reference to this the other day and said he did not think it should be brought in under this legislation, that there were more effective ways of dealing with it.

It seems to me that when a company, whether it be a rubber company, automobile company or any other, abuses a privilege action should be taken, and taken immediately. There is no reason why tires in this country should sell for $37, $38 and $39 when exactly the same tires are being sold in the United States at exactly one-half the price. In many cases the raw materials come from the same source. The same thing can be said about automobiles. Why should we in Canada have to pay $500, $600 or $700 more for a car identical to the ones made in the United States? These cars are manufactured by the same companies. Labour is cheaper in this country than in the United States and, as I said, in the case of tires the raw material comes from the same source. The same can be said in the -case of radios and refrigerators.

,Social Credit,,Charles Edward Johnston,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=c2d813a5-a966-4bb3-ae3f-2aa943b5d543&Language=E&Section=ALL

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Stanley Howard Knowles,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693541,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.70,1952-06-11,c2d813a5-a966-4bb3-ae3f-2aa943b5d543,ca.m.2582,Mr. Johnston:,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"I think too little emphasis has been placed on the control of monopolies. There have been some prosecutions in the past. There was a prosecution of the glass industry. They did not even bother to defend the case. They said: Sure we are guilty, we created a combine, we set prices, and so what? The court imposed a fine of $10,000. Isn't that ridiculous? They would have made more than that in a week's business, and the price of glass has not been affected one bit. Other combines have been prosecuted, found guilty and fined, but what effect has it had in the lowering of prices? Not one bit. Therefore our legislation must be defective in some way. The government has not taken any steps to see that prices were lowered as a result of these prosecutions and convictions. I know about the price maintenance legislation, and in general I
Combines Investigation Act think it was a good thing; but so far as combines are concerned something more drastic must be done.

The committee pointed out two very essential things that could be done, making use of the tariff and making use of the patent rights which these companies possess. I am disappointed that the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) has overlooked that important part of the committee's recommendations and, as the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair) has said, has in effect taken the teeth out of the legislation, something that is vitally needed. There are very few large concerns in this country that have no suspicion of monopolistic control about them. If we allow that situation to continue there is nothing that will destroy free enterprise faster. If we want to maintain the system which we think is the proper one and which has given such good results, then we must guard it very zealously.

1693547,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.76,1952-06-11,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. Fleming:,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,"ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"The present act provides for the initiation of an inquiry in three ways, one of which is on the complaint of six persons who are British subjects resident in Canada. It is proposed to change that to read, ""any six persons, Canadian citizens, resident in Canada."" Why should the language of the present act be narrowed? Surely if there are any reasons to suspect the existence of a combine we want to encourage persons to lay the available information before the director of investigation, and surely it does not matter whether or not they are Canadian citizens. The important thing is the information they put before the director, and as long as they are responsible persons and

Combines Investigation Act are British subjects resident in Canada of the full age of 21 years I should think that is good enough to qualify them to make their representations to the director. It will then be up to the director to decide whether the evidence is strong enough to warrant investigation. Why confine it to people who are Canadian citizens as well as having these other qualifications?

,Progressive Conservative,,Donald Methuen Fleming,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693548,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.77,1952-06-11,cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b,ca.m.7981,Mr. Garson:,Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"I do not think there is actually any narrowing of the subject matter at all. If my hon. friend will look at the old section 11 which is printed on the opposite pages he will see that it reads as follows:
11. (1) Any six persons, British subjects, resident in Canada, of the full age of 21 years . . .
The changing of the term to ""Canadian citizens"" is simply a reflection of the enactment of the Canadian Citizenship Act. It is a consequential change.

,Liberal,,Stuart Sinclair Garson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693549,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.78,1952-06-11,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. Fleming:,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"It goes a good deal farther than that. I do not think the minister has grasped the point I am making. There can be persons who are British subjects resident in Canada and who are not Canadian citizens. Surely we wish to encourage people who have knowledge of the existence of combines to make these facts available to the director of investigation; then why confine it to Canadian citizens? There may be British subjects resident in Canada who have not yet qualified for Canadian citizenship because they have not been here the full five years but nevertheless have information of the kind sought here and be in a position, except for this proposed amendment, to put it before the director. The effect of the amendment is to narrow the class of persons who can make a complaint to the director. I cannot see any justification for narrowing the kind of persons who can make these complaints. If we want to encourage complaints I think we should be widening the class of persons and not narrowing it. The effect of the proposed amendment is to eliminate British subjects resident in Canada 21 years of age and over who are not yet Canadian citizens.

,Progressive Conservative,,Donald Methuen Fleming,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693550,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.79,1952-06-11,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Knowles:,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"Instead of changing ""British subjects"" to ""Canadian citizens"" I wonder if the minister would consider deleting that phrase altogether so it would read, ""any six persons resident in Canada"". I realize the point the minister is making, namely that what the drafters thought they were doing was simply bringing the language up to date in view of the enactment of the Canadian Citizenship Act. I would agree to that, but if the point made by the hon. member for Eglinton has to be considered then we would want the wording to extend not only to residents in Canada who are British subjects
but not Canadian citizens but also to others who happen to be here for the required length of time.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Stanley Howard Knowles,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693551,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.80,1952-06-11,cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b,ca.m.7981,Mr. Garson:,Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"I do not think in actual practice it will make very much difference in any case that is likely to arise. In point of fact over the years the occasions upon which this section has been invoked have been very limited. It does seem that where the results of the action taken by six Canadian citizens may put the suspected company to a very great deal of expense and inconvenience, even if ultimately no case is found against the company, it is not at all unreasonable to limit that to Canadian citizens. If in a given case we will say that six persons who are not Canadian citizens come across a flagrant set of facts, it does not seem likely they would have much difficulty in finding six Canadian citizens whom they could get to sponsor their case for them. I think we are labouring a point that, in practice, is not of very great importance.

1693554,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.83,1952-06-11,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. Fleming:,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,"ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"There is a point I should like to raise here which applies not only to this section but to sections 10 and 12. It is the confining of the application to an ex parte basis, that is to say the application of the director to the commission or a member of it. We have a similar provision in section 9, subsection 2; in section 10, subsections 3 and 5 and in section 12, subsection 1. In every case the director makes an ex parte application to a member of the commission for the various orders that are provided for here. I am wondering if it is not feasible, in at least some of these cases, to make the application on notice to the party affected. Is there any great harm in these cases in making the application on notice?

,Progressive Conservative,,Donald Methuen Fleming,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693555,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.84,1952-06-11,cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b,ca.m.7981,Mr. Garson:,Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"We are asking the director,

under the new bill, to make these ex parte applications for permission to take steps which the commissioner, under the old act, has the power to take on his own initiative. We are, therefore, already imposing some restrictions upon the discretion of the director in that respect. I believe it would be unwise

to do so upon notice, because if it were upon notice then there would have to be a hearing before the director could move at all. During the delay caused thereby the documents or information which were sought might become unavailable. I think that what we have provided is the utmost precaution that we should insert in the present bill.

,Liberal,,Stuart Sinclair Garson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693556,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.85,1952-06-11,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. Fleming:,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"This calls for some comment. Under the proposed new structure the commission has certain powers that -the minister described last night as quasi-judicial. I think it is desirable that the judicial functions of the members of the commission be emphasized as much as possible. In each of these cases where provision is made for an application to the commission by the director, they are fairly serious matters.

For instance, section 9, subsection 2, relates to the demand for written returns which can be compelled by an order issued by a member of the commission on an ex parte application by the director. Under section 10, subsection 3, it is an order authorizing entry upon the premises of a person. Under subsection 5 of section 10, it is a provision for directing a police officer or constable to -take steps in order to guarantee an authorized representative admission or access to the premises. I shall not deal with the other one for the moment. It strikes me that when importance is attached to the judicial functions of the commission, regard should be had to the possibility of giving notice before an order is applied for under these various sections. They will be appointed for a term of ten years in order to give them security of tenure in their

positions. They will be lawyers, economists or professionally trained men or women of that sort who, in addition to a good academic training, have as much experience as we can secure in the candidates who present themselves. I expect that it may take a little bit of time to get people who are in every way suitable for these positions because we would rate them, as I am sure my hon. friend suspects, on a par with a judge in the courts. They are going to be discharging quasijudicial functions of an exceedingly onerous character. We had considered and had rejected the idea that the commission should be representative of, say, the farm, labour, consumer or the producer viewpoint, upon the ground that, unless we had a very large commission, it would be impossible to have represented upon it all the viewpoints which perhaps it would be thought should be represented on a commission that was set up on the basis of occupational representation. What justification is there for doubling this period?

,Progressive Conservative,,Donald Methuen Fleming,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693581,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.109,1952-06-11,cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b,ca.m.7981,Mr. Garson:,Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"I do not think that I could bring forward a better concrete example to support the proposed increase of this period than the rubber report which I tabled quite recently. The present period is 15 days. All that the present commissioner or the new commission is required to do in order to comply with his duty imposed under the old act or under the new bill is to attend at my office and tender to me a typewritten copy of that report. If they do that, then I have to give it some consideration and arrange for its reproduction by some mechanical means. As a matter of fact, that report which was tabled the other day was run off in the department and it took, on quite a good machine, about 12 days to reproduce 200 copies of it.

I suggest that three days of a difference is an altogether inadequate time allowance for a minister to receive a document of that sort and be under a statutory obligation to have it published. You cannot publish a report of that sort, in any fairness to a proper consideration of the public interest, by simply bringing here a couple of typewritten copies and leaving them on the table. If we are going to do the type of job in that respect which the act contemplates and get proper publicity for it, we must make sure that when the report is tabled there are an adequate number of copies and of press releases to service the press gallery; because it is only through the medium of the newspapers of this country that any of our activities in this house are brought to the attention of the people. To table two copies of this report and leave it to the press to come down, look through those copies and prepare their material would be out of the question altogether. When you see the mechanical difficulty which is involved in properly publishing this report, getting it out in such a way that the public interest will really be informed upon the subject matter, that 15 days is an altogether inadequate period. I do not think 30 days is by any means too much; but in any event, in what way can the public interest be prejudiced in having the publication made adequately within the period of 30 days? There is only a difference of between 15 and 30.
As matters stand now, any commissioner or any chairman of a commission, if he took 55704-198

Combines Investigation Act a dislike to the minister, could put him in an utterly impossible position by taking a typewritten copy of the report and leaving it on his desk. Then the minister will have a desperately hard time ever getting it published properly within the 15-day period. That is not a situation which I think should obtain and I very strongly urge that we leave the 30-day period as it is.

,Liberal,,Stuart Sinclair Garson,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693582,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.110,1952-06-11,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. Fleming:,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"It is quite evident that the publication does not involve any act on the part of the minister. He is not obliged to sift through that report and reach any fundamental decision in regard to it. All the statute requires of him is that he should make the report public within 15 days. The minister has given a rather striking example. The report which he tabled a week ago Monday, June 2, on the rubber combine was voluminous, and undoubtedly the task of multigraphing it was heavy. But this provision was written into the act for a definite purpose, namely to make sure that when reports are made by the commissioner under the old act they are not pigeonholed but are promptly made public. The language of section 27, subsection 5, of the present act is mandatory, and that time limit was put there for a very good purpose.

1693611,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.139,1952-06-11,5b04fb13-968f-4dac-80f6-3b569378e120,ca.m.5224,Mr. Fleming:,,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"Mr. Chairman, there is a point I should like to raise which would apply to several sections equally. I would refer to the proposed new section 32, and several of those following. We find the same thing at page 21 of the bill, in sections 498 and 498A of the Criminal Code. My observations will apply equally to all of them.

In these cases where, up to the present time, there has been provision for both fine and imprisonment by way of penalty for offences under the Combines Investigation Act, or these two sections of the Criminal Code, it is now proposed to eliminate any provision whatever for fines and to provide for penalties only by way of imprisonment. I wonder if that may not be likely to defeat the purpose in mind. I think all hon. members realize the purpose, and subscribe to the aim of making these penal sections stiff, so that when some person is convicted of an offence under the Combines Investigation Act, or under these two sections of the Criminal Code, a real punishment will be imposed, and so that those who may be contemplating becoming breakers of these laws will hesitate to do so, in the knowledge that they are rendering themselves subject to imprisonment. I am wondering, though, if there is not another consideration which ought to be taken into account. It may be that cases will arise where the degree of guilt does not greatly impress the court and where, if the court had power as it has at present, it would impose a fine. However, lacking the power to impose a fine and being faced only with power to impose imprisonment, it may be found that in these cases courts would simply impose suspended sentences.
Has serious consideration been given by the law officers of the Department of Justice
Combines Investigation Act

to this step of completely eliminating any provision for fines? I am not arguing for small fines, or the kind of fines that would not act as a very effective sanction in cases of this kind. As was done previously, let us make -the possible fine a substantial amount. But is it desirable to tie the hands of a court in the way in which these amendments undoubtedly will tie its hands?

And since obviously most cases that arise under the Combines Investigation Act involve corporations which cannot be imprisoned, the court must impose a fine. The effect of the bill now before the committee is to remove the existing ceiling of $25,000 upon the fine imposed for offences against this act. 1693615,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.143,1952-06-11,103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78,ca.m.7989,Mr. Knowles:,Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"I was waiting for a later section to raise a point I have in mind, but perhaps it is related to section 32 and might well be raised now in view of the discussion that has taken place. The minister has just remarked that you cannot put a corporation in jail, but I remind him that there is another statute-I forget just which one it is-containing a provision that if directors of a company are parties to a certain offence they may be put in jail personally. That is also true under this legislation in respect of certain offences. For example, section 38, subsection 3 provides:

Where a corporation commits an offence against subsection one or two any director or officer of such corporation who assents to or acquiesces in the offence committed by the corporation shall be guilty of that offence personally and cumulatively with the corporation and with his co-directors or associate officers.

When one looks at subsections 1 and 2 of that section he finds that a fine or imprisonment is possible, but it is also to be noted that the offences referred to are only offences against the sections that require co-operation in preparing reports or obtaining information. As the minister knows, one of my colleagues, the hon. member for Assiniboia, has

actually brought up this question in the form of a public bill in which it is suggested that the wording of section 38, subsection 3, might include offences against section 32, which is the section we are now discussing, as well as against the subsections already covered.

Section 32 is the really important section. It makes it an offence to assist knowingly in the formation or operation of a combine. It seems to me that if we are going to put teeth in this legislation it is just as important, if not more important, to make it an offence for which a director of a corporation may be put in jail because he knowingly assisted in the formation of a combine, as it is to make it an offence to withhold co-operation in getting information for a report.

My suggestion is that when we get to section 38, subsection 3, there should be included as well a reference to section 32 in addition to the reference to subsections 1 and 2. Similarly when we get to section 498A I submit that a proviso should be added to the effect that where a corporation is involved the terms of section 38, subsection 3, might apply. No doubt the minister has given thought to this and I dare to hope that even though it has not yet come forward he has considered the bill standing in the name of the hon. member for Assiniboia. I should like to hear his comments on this matter.

1693616,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.144,1952-06-11,cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b,ca.m.7981,Mr. Garson:,Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"If my hon. friend will look at section 32, subsection 1, he will find that it reads as follows:
Every person-
That includes a corporation or an individual.

-who is a party or privy to or knowingly assists in the formation or operation of a combine is guilty of an indictable offence and liable on conviction to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years.

That means that under that section Mr. John Jones, who is a director or manager or official of an accused corporation, could be named in the indictment as a person responsible for knowingly assisting in the formation of a combine. But when we are considering whether we should so charge him, we must consider what effect it will have upon the course of the trial. Sometimes the proving of a case against an accused corporation may depend in some degree upon the evidence given by someone like John Jones, and it may not be advisable to name him in the indictment. If he were accused he might plead not guilty, and then he could not be called as a witness against either himself or the accused corporation.
My hon. friend will recall when we were amending the act, I think two years ago, it was provided that in all cases where a

charge was laid against a corporation that it should not have a jury trial but should proceed before a judge. In most cases that is more convenient. My hon. friend will recall that the case of the alleged bread combine in western Canada took up 100 court days. He can imagine how impossible it would be to keep jurymen away from their occupations for 100 court days, which might mean nearly six months of actual time. It would be impossible to obtain the proper consideration by a jury preoccupied with getting away to their own occupations. That was one reason for that amendment. Yet if we charge an individual he can elect a jury trial.

Those are considerations which have to be taken into account by the prosecutor when he launches his prosecution. The fact that individuals are not prosecuted is not because of any hole in the law under which they escape liability; it is simply that it is considered that this may be the best way to accomplish the conviction of the accused corporation.

,Co-operative Commonwealth Federation (C.C.F.),,Stanley Howard Knowles,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=103e48f0-b6bb-43eb-9c06-7ceffaf3ea78&Language=E&Section=ALL
1693618,ca.proc.d.1952-06-11.27.1.146,1952-06-11,cd8bfdc8-48c2-4679-9567-c4c801d7b82b,ca.m.7981,Mr. Garson:,Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada,COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT TO PROVIDE FOR ADMINISTRATION,ESTABLISH- MENT OF RESTRICTIVE TRADE PRACTICES COMMISSION, ETC.",,"Section 38, subsection 2, reads:

Every person who, without good and sufficient cause, the proof whereof lies on him, refuses, neglects or fails to comply with a notice in writing requiring a written return under oath or affirmation, pursuant to section nine or subsection two of section twenty-two is guilty of an offence and liable on summary conviction or on conviction on indictment to a fine of not more than five thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years or to both.

That is a case where the investigator goes into ABC company and wants to get some information, and the people there adopt an attitude of resistance and non-co-operation. They would make themselves liable under this section. That is an easy offence to prove and there would be no particular difficulty in laying a charge against an official of the company under those circumstances. But the offence of a combine under section 32, subsection 1, is in most cases very difficult to prove because of the great complexities and thousands of exhibits that might be involved. So far as the rubber report is concerned, there were 8,000 pages of evidence and 4,000 exhibits, and that is before we get into the case at all. If in any case of that sort the man who has the very onerous

Combines Investigation Act responsibility of advising a prosecution feels that some individual is a key witness in the case he will hesitate very much about making him a defendant because he is more use as a witness than as a defendant. But it is not through any deficiency in the law. The law is as plain as a pikestaff. Every person who is a party or privy to or knowingly assists in the formation or operation of a combine is guilty of an indictable offence, whether it is a person who is a corporation or a person who is an individual.
